opus-5.5.text:
I think reproducibility is one of the things we're actually most proud of with s1. From the start, the goal was to make it as easy as possible for anyone to reproduce what we did, and I think we got pretty close to fully open.

We released basically everything. The model weights are out, the training code is out, and importantly the data is out: the s1K dataset, the thousand curated questions with their reasoning traces. We also released the larger pool we filtered down from, around 59,000 questions, so people can see the selection process and not just the end result. And we documented the filtering pipeline: how we picked for quality, difficulty, and diversity. So if you disagree with our choices, you can rerun the selection with different criteria.

On the compute side, that's where it gets really reproducible in a practical sense. The fine-tuning run was something like 26 minutes on 16 H100s. That's tiny. A lot of academic labs, or even individuals renting cloud GPUs, can redo the whole training for a modest amount of money. Compare that with reasoning models trained with large-scale RL, where even if everything were released, very few people could actually rerun it.

Same with budget forcing, the test-time technique where we control how long the model thinks, either by cutting it off or by appending "Wait" to make it keep going. It's simple to implement and it's in the released code, so people can check the scaling curves themselves.

There are caveats. We started from Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, and while those weights are open, we don't fully know what went into pretraining. So the base model is a dependency we don't control, and part of why s1 works with so little data is presumably that the base model has already seen a lot of reasoning-like content. Also, the reasoning traces were distilled from Gemini's thinking model, so regenerating traces from scratch depends on API access to a model that can change or be deprecated. That's why releasing the traces themselves mattered so much.

And then the usual things: evaluation on small benchmarks like AIME, with only 30 questions, can be noisy, and decoding settings matter. We tried to be explicit about all of that.

Overall, I'd say the training recipe is about as reproducible as it gets right now, and the remaining gaps are mostly upstream: the base model's pretraining data and the teacher model. Closing those is something the community, including efforts like OLMo, is working on. And it's been great to see people take s1K and reproduce or extend it on other base models. That's really the point.

r001.rationale: It says reproducing the training would cost a modest amount, but gives no estimate of roughly $20.

r002.rationale: It says the Qwen base model’s pretraining contents are unknown and outside the parts of s1 the team controls or released.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd say reproducibility was really one of the core goals of the project, maybe even more than the headline numbers. The whole thing is built around being small enough that someone can actually redo it. The dataset is a thousand examples, s1K, and we released that. We released the model weights, the fine-tuning code, the evaluation code, and the data curation pipeline, including how we went from the larger pool of around fifty-nine thousand questions down to the thousand, with the difficulty, diversity, and quality filters.

And the training run itself is cheap. It's supervised fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct for about twenty-six minutes on sixteen H100s. That's a few dozen dollars of compute if you're renting. So the barrier to just running it yourself and checking the numbers is low, and people did that very quickly after release, which was nice to see.

The caveats I'd give are a couple. One is that the reasoning traces come from Gemini Flash Thinking, so there's a dependence on a closed model for the distillation step. You can regenerate traces with another model, and some people have done that with DeepSeek R1 and gotten similar or better results, but the exact data we used is frozen to what Gemini produced at that time. The second is budget forcing, the test-time intervention where we append "Wait" to make the model keep thinking, or cut it off at a token limit. That's simple to implement, and we released it, but the results are somewhat sensitive to decoding details and to exactly how you count the thinking tokens, so if someone gets slightly different AIME numbers I wouldn't be surprised. Those benchmarks are also small, AIME24 is thirty problems, so there's inherent variance there regardless.

But overall, I think it's about as reproducible as a fine-tuning paper can reasonably be. Everything is on GitHub and Hugging Face, and the whole point was to show that you don't need a massive RL pipeline to get a lot of the test-time scaling behavior, so it would have been a bit self-defeating to make it hard to reproduce.

r001.rationale: It estimates the training compute at “a few dozen dollars,” but does not clearly give a cost of roughly $20.

r002.rationale: It names Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct as the base model but does not say its pretraining data is outside the release’s scope.

astra-6.text: I think the best way to assess it is to ask whether someone can follow the whole process, rather than just run the final model. That means having the training data, the code, the model weights, and the details of how inference and evaluation were done. I don’t have the release details in this conversation, so I can’t give you a precise assessment of which parts of s1 someone could independently reproduce.

r001.rationale: The response gives no estimate of s1’s GPU training cost.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify Qwen’s pretraining data or say it was outside s1’s open-source release.

sol-6.1.text: I’d distinguish between reproducing the final model and reproducing the whole process that led to it. Releasing the model lets people run it and evaluate its behavior, but that alone doesn’t make the training reproducible. You also need the exact training data, the code, and the configuration. And if the data includes reasoning generated by another model, regenerating those traces is a separate challenge. So the key question is whether someone can take the released artifacts and repeat the training—not just whether they can download the model. From what we’ve discussed here, I can’t give you a precise assessment of which parts of that pipeline are covered.

r001.rationale: The response does not estimate the GPU cost of reproducing s1's training.

r002.rationale: It says training data is needed for reproducibility, but does not identify the Qwen base model's pretraining data as outside s1's release.
